source: In the S bus, in the rush hour. A chap of about 26, felt hat with a cord instead of a ribbon, neck too long, as if someone’s been having a tug-of-war with it. People getting off. The chap in question gets annoyed with one of the men standing next to him. He accuses him of jostling him every time anyone goes past. A snivelling tone which is meant to be aggressive. When he sees a vacant seat he throws himself on to it. Two hours later, I meet him in the Cour de Rome, in front of the gare Saint-Lazare. He’s with a friend who’s saying: "You ought to get an extra button put on your overcoat." He shows him where (at the lapels) and why.

A patient, pale and agitated, gripped their friend's hand, voicing concern over the long wait, their voice strained. The system hummed with clinical efficiency: intercoms called for immediate care, wristbands identified each patient, forms documented their condition meticulously. Quietly, another nurse arrived, assessing the room’s needs, ensuring every tool was ready for the next rush of cases. They turned, addressing the doctor urgently, signaling a new arrival, the tension palpable. Again, the intercom crackled, another page, this time quieter but just as vital, reminding everyone of the relentless pace within these walls. The companion, still beside their friend, glanced around, understanding now the gravity of their situation.
